Moon

Two months hide inside every lunar month. This is the figure that tells them apart.

Pause all animations

Two Months

Let's start a clock at new Moon. The dotted grey line points at a distant star that never moves; the orange arrow points at the Sun and creeps along as Earth travels its own orbit.

Move the slider until the grey Moon returns to the dotted star line. That takes 27.32 days, one sidereal month, the time for one lap measured against the distant stars: 27 days, 7 hours, and 43 minutes. But the orange Sun direction has crept ahead, so the Moon needs two more days to line up with it again: 29.53 days, one synodic month, the time between two new Moons, 29 days, 12 hours, and 44 minutes. The two rates subtract:

\frac{1}{\tok{sun}{T_{\mathrm{syn}}}} = \frac{1}{\tok{moon}{T_{\mathrm{sid}}}} - \frac{1}{\tok{star}{Y}}

Every lunar calendar counts the synodic month, and twelve of them fall eleven days short of a year, which is where the trouble starts.

Final words

Two clocks, one Moon.

Glossary
sidereal month ↩
The time for the Moon to complete one orbit measured against the distant stars: 27.322 days (27 d 7 h 43 m).
synodic month ↩
The time between two successive new Moons: 29.530 days (29 d 12 h 44 m). Longer than the sidereal month because Earth moves along its orbit meanwhile.
